id: Your Invitation to a Modest Breakfast

prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

It’s too cold to smoke outside, but if you come over, I’ll keep my hands to myself, or won’t I. I would like to tell you about the wall eaten up by the climbing plant—it was so beautiful. Various things have been happening to me, all of them sexual. The man on the bus took off his pants so I could see him better. Another man said, “Ignore him darlin’. Just sit on my lap.” But I’m not one of those who’s hungriest in the morning, unlike the man at the bakery who eats egg after egg after egg. Listen. Come over: the cold has already eaten the summer. I need another pair of ears: from the kitchen I can’t tell if I’m hearing wind chimes or some gray woman with failing arms dropping a pan full of onions and potatoes. This morning I need four hands— two to wash the greens, one to lift a teakettle, one to pour the milk. This morning, one little mouth will not do. We could play a game where we crouch on the tiles, two yellow dogs drinking coffee from bowls. We could play a game where we let the breakfast burn. Outside there’s a world where every love scene begins with a man in a doorway; he walks over to the woman and says “Open your mouth.”

**Come Over**

Come over, I want to say, now that the cold has settled into the streets and the windows fog with the breath of strangers. Come over, and I promise to keep my hands to myself, to be good, to keep the distance I claim to want. But even as I offer the invitation, I feel the pull of something I cannot name—the ambivalence and the desire tangled together, so that I no longer know whether I am asking for company or for surrender.

The cold has done nothing to keep them away. All winter, the encounters have found me: men who step too close on empty platforms, men who unzip themselves in the gray light of afternoon buses, men who mistake my silence for an opening. Their advances arrive uninvited, one after another, until they blur into a single unwelcome presence that follows me home and lingers in the doorway of my thoughts. I did not ask for any of it, and yet it keeps happening, as though the world has decided what my body is for.

What I want is so much simpler than what I am given. I am lonely in a way that has settled into the bones, a hollowness that aches for another person—not for possession, but for presence. I want someone else's ears to hear the small things I say at the end of the day. I want another pair of hands beside mine, warm and ordinary. I want the weight of a body in the room, the proof that I am not alone in it.

I imagine the mornings most of all. I picture myself cracking eggs into a bowl, buttering bread, pouring coffee into two cups instead of one. There is someone at the table, half-awake, and the steam rises between us, and none of it is remarkable—which is exactly why I long for it. To share the plain, unglamorous rituals of a morning is to be known by someone, to belong to a life larger than my solitude.

And yet, when I reach for an image of love, what surfaces is not tenderness but command. I see a man telling a woman to open her mouth, and I understand that this, too, is how romance has been written for me—as instruction, as control, as the woman receiving what the man decides to give. My yearning for gentle, equal companionship stands against this darker vision, and I am left wondering whether the two can ever be pulled apart, or whether every invitation I offer already carries the shape of someone else's hand.

# On Loneliness and Longing: An Analysis

This poem explores themes of loneliness, desire, and domestic longing through a speaker who reaches out across the empty space between two people. The invitation that anchors the work—a simple call for another person to come over—becomes the emotional center around which everything else orbits. Yet what surrounds this invitation is anything but simple. The speaker recounts fragmented, often unsettling sexual encounters, memories that surface without clear chronology or resolution, interspersed with the mundane details of morning rituals: coffee cooling in a cup, light coming through a window, the ordinary motions of a body moving through an empty apartment.

The tension between these registers—the raw and the routine—creates the poem's distinctive atmosphere. Rather than presenting intimacy as comforting, the speaker allows it to feel disjointed and haunted, as though physical closeness has failed to deliver the connection it seemed to promise. The unsettling quality of the remembered encounters suggests a hunger that sex alone cannot satisfy, a reaching toward something that remains just out of grasp.

The work's power lies in this juxtaposition of intimacy and isolation. The imagery of shared breakfast—a table set for two, food prepared and offered—carries an ache of domestic longing, the desire for an ordinary life shared with another person. Meanwhile, the recurring image of multiplied body parts, hands and mouths and limbs appearing in excess, transforms the human form into something both abundant and fragmented, present and disassembled. These bodies seem to proliferate precisely because no single, whole presence exists to fill the speaker's need.

Through these techniques, the poem conveys a deep hunger for genuine human connection. What the speaker wants is not merely company or physical satisfaction, but the wholeness that comes from being truly known and accompanied. The invitation extended throughout the poem thus reads less as an offer of pleasure than as a plea against solitude—an attempt to close the distance between two isolated people through the small, hopeful gesture of asking someone to stay.

# The Beauty of Variety in Everyday Life

**The** world we live in is full of endless possibilities, each waiting to be discovered. When we open our eyes to what surrounds us, we begin to notice just how much there is to explore and appreciate.

## Embracing Various Perspectives

**Various** cultures, ideas, and traditions shape the way we understand our existence. No single viewpoint holds all the answers, which is why remaining open to different perspectives enriches our lives. People from diverse backgrounds bring **various** talents, stories, and solutions to the challenges we face together. This diversity is not a weakness but a tremendous strength.

Consider the countless ways individuals approach a single problem. One person might rely on logic, while **another** trusts intuition. **The** combination of these approaches often produces results far greater than any single method could achieve alone.

## Moving From One Idea to Another

Growth happens when we allow ourselves to transition from one experience to **another**. Life is rarely a straight line; instead, it winds through **various** stages, each teaching us something new. **The** lessons we learn in one chapter prepare us for **another** that follows.

Every ending is simply the beginning of **another** journey. When one door closes, **another** frequently opens, offering fresh opportunities we never anticipated.

## The Value of Reflection

**The** ability to pause and reflect allows us to appreciate how far we have come. By examining **various** moments of our past and imagining **another** possible future, we gain clarity about who we truly are and who we hope to become.

In the end, **the** richness of life lies in its variety—in the countless choices, connections, and chances that make each day unique.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a prose poem in a conversational, intimate voice—someone inviting a lover over on a cold morning. Blend domestic imagery (breakfast, greens, teakettle) with unsettling sexual encounters and surreal touches.
counterfactuals.output:
Come Over Before It Gets Light

Come over while the frost is still writing its illegible letters on the glass. I have been awake since the dark part of the morning, waiting the way a kettle waits—patient, then suddenly screaming. Don't knock. The door has been unlocked since the idea of you.

I'll make eggs. I'll make them the way you like, which is to say I'll break them and something will look back at me from the pan, and we'll agree not to mention it. There are greens on the counter, still gritty with the field they came from, still cold as the necks of swans. I've been washing them and washing them. The water runs and runs and I can't get the soil to admit it's finished.

Take off your coat. Take off the weather you brought with you. I want to see the animal of your spine, the way it curves when you reach for the sugar and pretend you don't know I'm watching. Last night I dreamed your mouth was full of small blue flowers and when you spoke they fell out and rooted in the floorboards and by morning the whole kitchen was a meadow and I was afraid to walk anywhere.

Come here. Let me put my cold hands somewhere warm. Let me forget which of us is the guest. The kettle is singing that high note that means the water has given up being water. Outside, the birds are doing something violent to the last of the berries. Inside, I want to press my ear to your chest and hear the machinery, the little factory that makes you keep choosing this, keep choosing the frost and the eggs and the strange soft trouble of my company.

The toast is burning. Let it. Some mornings the smoke is the closest thing we have to incense. Come closer. There is a whole day out there we've decided not to attend. Let them mark us absent. Let the greens go warm and limp in the colander like something that has finally, finally been convinced.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a poem addressed to a lover, using an inviting yet unsettling tone, that mixes mundane morning tasks with strange erotic anecdotes and imagery of cold eating the summer.
counterfactuals.output:
# Frost in the Toaster

Come here, love—the kettle's screaming
like the woman in my dream
who wore your hands as gloves.
The coffee's black. The window's fogged
with something breathing back.

Butter the toast. I watched you sleep
and counted all the ways
the summer's leaving us:
the basil browning on the sill,
the way your mouth
tastes faintly now of snow.

Remember the orchard?
How you pressed a peach against my throat
and told me *this is how the cold begins*—
sweetness first, then the slow white teeth
closing on the season's fruit.

Bring your slippers. Bring the strange
soft animal of your yawn.
There's ice inside the marmalade.
There's a stranger in the mirror
wearing your good morning like a wound.

I love you like the frost
loves the last warm thing it finds—
completely, and with ruin.
So sit. Eat. Let me
comb the winter from your hair
while the eggs go cold
and something summer in us
finally stops singing.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a free-verse prose poem where the speaker asks someone to come over for breakfast, describing weird sexual things happening to her and imagining playing games like being two dogs drinking coffee from bowls.
counterfactuals.output:
Come Over, I've Made Something

Come over, I've made something of the morning—cracked it open like the eggs I keep forgetting on the counter, their yolks going warm and strange, like everything else in this apartment lately.

Come over. My body has been doing peculiar things without asking me. Last night my spine unspooled like a ribbon of pasta and I laughed so hard the ceiling blushed. I want to tell you about it over toast. I want to watch you not believe me while the butter melts into little golden confessions.

Come over and be a dog with me. Let's forget our thumbs. Let's get down on the linoleum and lap coffee from blue bowls, tongues clumsy and ridiculous, our human dignity left folded on a chair like yesterday's clothes. You be the shaggy one who knocks over the cream. I'll be the one who howls at the toaster.

Something is happening to me that I don't have words for yet, so I'm inventing them: the way my skin feels electric-adjacent, the way desire has become a kind of weather I move through, humid and full of small lightnings. Come translate me. Come sit at my sticky table.

We could play at being animals until we forget we were ever pretending. We could name the sunlight after cities we'll never visit. We could let the eggs go completely to ruin.

Just come over. The coffee's hot. The floor is cold and waiting. I've set out two bowls.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate an experimental poem in the style of contemporary confessional poets—loose, associative, sexual, domestic, with lines like needing four hands to make breakfast.
counterfactuals.output:
**Domestic Interior with Two Bodies**

Some mornings I need four hands
to make breakfast—two to crack
the eggs, two to hold your face
still while I decide
whether to forgive you.

The kitchen light is a confession
I never asked for. Butter
softening on the counter
like an argument we abandoned
halfway, both of us too tired
to be right.

I keep finding your hair
in the strangest places—
the drain, the book I'm not reading,
the small of my own back
where you left it last night
like a signature.

There is a language spoken only
between the sheets and the hip,
a wet grammar,
your mouth conjugating me
into first person, present tense,
*I am, I am, I am*—

and then the coffee burns,
and I am the woman
who forgot the coffee again,
who stands at the window
half-dressed, holding a knife
and a peach,
deciding which one
the day deserves.

We are so ordinary
it terrifies me. The way
you fold the laundry
into perfect surrenders.
The way I bite you
just to leave proof
I was here.

Love is mostly
picking up after the body—
its spills, its appetites,
its little deaths on the mattress,
its need to be fed
and fed
and fed.

I would use all four hands
if I had them.
I would grow more.
I would become
an animal of arms
just to hold the morning
and you
and the eggs
before they break.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write something that reads like a needy, flirtatious morning monologue-poem full of surreal juxtapositions: men on buses, a bakery, wind chimes, burnt breakfast, and a doorway command to "open your mouth."
counterfactuals.output:
Morning Inventory, or Please

The men on the bus are all wearing your face today—
did you plant them there? Little seeds of you
rattling past my window at 7 a.m.,
each one refusing to wave back.
That's fine. That's fine. I'm not counting.

The bakery two streets over is breathing again,
exhaling yeast into the whole neighborhood
like it's got something to prove,
and I hate how much I want to be dough in your hands,
kneaded, punished, left to rise.
Is that too much before coffee? It's too much.
I'll say it anyway. I'm saying it.

There are wind chimes somewhere
having a nervous breakdown,
and I've decided they're doing it for me,
a little brass orchestra of my restlessness,
clanging out the word your name spells backwards.

I burned the eggs. Of course I burned the eggs.
I was thinking about your wrists
and the pan went the color of a bad decision.
Black lace of breakfast, offered to no one.
I'd feed it to you if you asked.
Ask me. Ask me for the ruined thing.

And you—
standing in the doorway like weather,
like a sentence I didn't finish—
you look at me and say
open your mouth,

and God help me,
I forget every argument I've ever won.
I forget the burnt eggs,
the bus full of counterfeit yous,
the chimes still losing their minds in the yard.

Open your mouth.

Okay.
Yes.
Tell me what goes in.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
